Lorraine Hansberry. The playwright whose debut A Raisin in the Sun became the first play by an African-American woman to reach Broadway, marking a watershed moment for Black representation in American theater.

A Raisin in the Sun premiered in 1959 and won the New York Drama Critics Circle Award. It tells the story of the Younger family in Chicago, with each member possessing competing dreams as they confront racism and economic hardship. The title derives from Langston Hughes's poem Harlem, which asks what happens to a dream deferred, a question that animates the entire drama.

Hansberry's work was groundbreaking for centering Black family complexity and inner conflict rather than portraying Black life as primarily a victim narrative. She also wrote the television play The Drinking Gourd in 1960, which examined slavery, and began work on other pieces that explored the historical and political dimensions of Black experience. Beyond her drama, she published essays and speeches engaging with American politics, the Civil Rights movement, and the role of the artist in social movements.

Hansberry died of cancer at age thirty-four, cutting short what promised to be a luminous theatrical career. Yet the work she left behind left an indelible mark on American drama, and her legacy connects her to James Baldwin, who was similarly engaged with theater and essays during the Civil Rights era, and to the broader lineage of Black writers like Gwendolyn Brooks and Langston Hughes who brought vernacular and dignity to the American stage.
